summaries.example: Imagine a science machine checking whether a tiny object has spin-up or spin-down. In the usual account, the machine quickly chooses one result. In Everett's account, the wave description keeps both connected possibilities. Each relative record can contain a clear result, even though the whole description contains more than one record.
summaries.summary: Quantum mechanics has a puzzle about measurements. Its usual rules describe a system changing smoothly, but they also add a special collapse when a measurement occurs. If the measuring person and machine are physical systems too, these rules can conflict. Hugh Everett proposed dropping collapse. His pure wave mechanics lets the whole system continue smoothly. A measurement then creates connected parts of the description in which different observers have different definite records. Everett called these relative states. He also tried to explain ordinary quantum statistics by saying that typical sequences of records have the familiar patterns. The entry emphasizes an important limit: typicality is not exactly the same as ordinary probability. Extra ideas may be needed to explain what a person should expect before a measurement.
key_ideas: The usual quantum theory uses smooth change when no measurement happens but a sudden collapse when a measurement happens.
Everett removed collapse and kept the smooth wave rule for every physical system, including observers and measuring tools.
After a measurement, different relative records can describe different results.
Everett argued that typical long sequences of records have the same statistics as ordinary quantum mechanics.
The source explains that this account is consistent, but it does not by itself give ordinary probabilities about which future result one should expect.
summaries.why_it_matters: This idea asks a basic question: should a scientific theory describe only the result we experience, or also the larger mathematical structure behind it? Everett's proposal removes a special rule and treats observers as part of the physical description. It also shows why explaining clear records and explaining probabilities are separate challenges.

important_terms.definition: A quantum description that can contain several possible states together before an observation.
A special change in the usual quantum theory where a set of possibilities suddenly becomes one result.
A record that is definite compared with one part of a larger connected system, even if the whole system has several connected records.
A way of measuring which patterns are common or usual among the different branches of a quantum description.

questions_to_think_about: Would a theory seem strange if it described more possibilities than we directly notice?
What is the difference between seeing one clear record and describing the whole system?
Does showing that a usual pattern is typical explain why you should expect it?

summaries.example: Consider an ideal observer measuring a two-state quantum system prepared in a superposition of spin-up and spin-down. Under collapse theory, the observer ends in one collapsed state, with the usual squared-amplitude probabilities. Under pure wave mechanics, linear evolution produces an entangled state containing an observer recording spin-up and an observer recording spin-down. Everett's relative-state idea treats each observer-record as determinate relative to its correlated system state. Across long sequences, a norm-squared measure makes the usual frequencies typical, but the theory alone does not establish ordinary forward-looking chances.
summaries.summary: Everettian quantum mechanics begins with a difficulty in the standard collapse formulation. Continuous linear dynamics applies when no measurement occurs, while a separate stochastic collapse is said to occur during measurement. If observers and devices are physical systems, applying these rules within a nested-measurement scenario can produce incompatible descriptions of the same composite system. Everett's response was pure wave mechanics: remove collapse and let linear dynamics govern everything. The resulting state can be an entangled superposition of different observer records. His relative-state formulation says that a definite record exists relative to a correlated component, even when there is no single determinate state for the subsystem considered independently. To address statistics, Everett introduced a typicality measure based on squared amplitudes and argued that, for long sequences, typical relative records display standard quantum frequencies and randomness. The entry stresses that this does not by itself yield ordinary probabilities about future outcomes or explain why an observer should expect to occupy a typical branch. Later reconstructions add further assumptions, including worlds, minds, or hidden variables.
key_ideas: Everett interprets the measurement problem as a conflict between continuous evolution and collapse, especially when measurements are nested inside larger measurements.
The relative-state formulation removes collapse and models observers as ordinary physical systems governed by the same linear dynamics.
The entangled post-measurement state does not have one determinate absolute record for the observer, but it contains determinate records relative to correlated components.
Everett's typicality argument uses a norm-squared measure over branches; it shows that typical record sequences approach the standard quantum frequencies.
The entry distinguishes empirical faithfulness from empirical adequacy: finding experienced records in the model is weaker than deriving ordinary probabilities for present or future outcomes.

Many-worlds, many-minds, and hidden-variable extensions add different assumptions to obtain richer accounts of records and probability; they should not simply be identified with Everett's original formulation.
summaries.why_it_matters: The proposal separates several questions often run together: how quantum states evolve, how observers obtain definite records, why records agree, and why outcomes have probabilistic statistics. It also illustrates a general philosophical issue about theories: logical consistency and a match with experience may not be enough for full predictive adequacy. Deciding what extra assumptions are justified is part of evaluating interpretations of quantum mechanics.

important_terms.definition: The standard formulation's sudden, probabilistic change from a superposition to one measurement outcome.
A formulation that keeps only the continuous, deterministic wave evolution and applies it to all physical systems.
The state assigned to one subsystem given a particular state of the rest of a composite system; it need not be an independent absolute state.
A state in which the states of parts are linked so that the whole cannot be represented as separate independent states.
A criterion for treating some branches or record sequences as overwhelmingly representative, calculated from squared amplitudes.
The standard quantum rule that assigns outcome weights using the squared magnitudes of amplitudes.
The requirement that a theory's model correspond appropriately to experienced records, even if it contains additional structure.
A stronger standard requiring a theory to provide ordinary predictions and expectations for observed outcomes.

questions_to_think_about: Does removing collapse solve the measurement problem, or does it shift the main problem to records and probability?
Why is a measure over branches not automatically a probability about which outcome an observer will experience?
What does it mean for a theory to be empirically faithful if it contains structure that observers do not normally notice?
Should later many-worlds theories be treated as interpretations of Everett's proposal or as additional theories built from it?

summaries.example: Suppose a robot checks a quantum object that might show red or blue. In the usual story, the quantum state collapses and the robot records one color. In Everett's story, the combined object-and-robot state keeps evolving smoothly. One part of that state contains a robot with a red record, and another contains a robot with a blue record. Each record is definite relative to its matching part of the object, although the complete description includes both.
summaries.summary: Everettian quantum mechanics is an attempt to solve the measurement problem in standard quantum theory. The standard account says that a quantum system changes smoothly most of the time but collapses to one result during measurement. This becomes puzzling when the observer and the measuring device are treated as physical systems too. In a nested-measurement thought experiment, one observer may describe a collapse while a larger observer describes smooth evolution, creating a conflict. Everett removes the collapse rule and keeps smooth wave evolution for every system. After a measurement, the whole state can be an entangled combination of different observer records. Everett's idea of a relative state allows each correlated part to contain a definite record, even though the whole state has no single ordinary record for the observer. He then uses a typicality measure, based on squared amplitudes, to argue that long sequences in typical branches show the usual quantum frequencies. The entry carefully distinguishes this from ordinary probability: the original proposal does not fully explain why a particular observer should expect one future result rather than another. Other versions add further assumptions to address that issue.
key_ideas: The measurement problem appears because the standard theory uses two different kinds of change: smooth evolution and collapse.
Everett treats the observer as part of the quantum system instead of placing the observer outside it.
A complete quantum state can contain several correlated records, while each relative observer has a definite record.
Everett uses typicality to explain why long records can look random and follow the usual quantum statistics.
Typicality is not automatically the same as probability, so critics ask whether the theory explains what an observer should expect before measuring.
Later proposals, such as many-worlds and many-minds approaches, add different ideas and should not be treated as identical.
summaries.why_it_matters: Everett's proposal changes the picture of what a measurement is. Instead of a special event that interrupts quantum evolution, measurement becomes an ordinary physical interaction. This makes the theory more uniform, but it creates new questions about definite experience and chance. Studying those trade-offs helps us understand why interpretations of quantum mechanics are philosophical as well as mathematical.

important_terms.definition: A quantum state that combines different possible results before a measurement.
The sudden selection of one result in the standard measurement theory.
The smooth rule that changes quantum states continuously and deterministically.
A state described in relation to another part of a larger system, rather than as an independent state.
A situation in which parts of a quantum system are linked so strongly that they cannot be fully described separately.
A rule for identifying which branches or record patterns count as common in Everett's account.
The familiar numerical pattern of quantum results, based on squared amplitudes.

questions_to_think_about: If a measuring device is physical, should it follow the same quantum rules as the object it measures?
Can several relative records be real without there being one single record for the entire system?
Is saying that a result is typical enough to explain why someone expects that result?
What extra assumptions might a theory need in order to explain future probabilities?
